# Our First Multilinear Regression Model!

First, load our data and create a model of mpg against weight, HP and drat:

```{r}
mlm <- lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp + drat, data = mtcars)
summary(mlm)
```

So, the computed model is:

$$mpg=29.394934-3.227954wt-0.032230hp+1.615049drat$$
The interpretation of the above formula is as follows:

* For 1000 lbs of additional weight, we run 3.227954 miles / gallon **less** *ceteris paribus* (c.p.).
* For 1 H of additional HP, we run 0.032230 miles / gallon **less** (c.p.).
* For a change of 1 in rear axle ratio, we run 1.615049 miles / gallon **more** (c.p.).
* For the (fictional) case of a car with 0 weight, 0 HP and 0 rear axle ratio, we run 29.394934 miles / gallon.


> In our context *ceteris paribus* means "all other parameters being the same".

To begin with, observe that $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ are good enough, accounting for more than $80\%$ of the 
total variance in our data. But, as you might well see, our $p$ values are not as strong as last time. Namely:

* For weight, we have a $p$ value of $0.000364$ which is good enough.
* For HP, we have a $p$ value of $0.001178$ which, again, is below common confidence thresholds of $0.05$ or $0.01$.
* For rear axle ratio we see that there is a really weak $p$ value of $0.198755$, which means that there is a $20\%$ chance that we make
a type I error, i.e., we erroneously reject the null hypothesis that there is no effect of drat of mpg (or the other way).

Also, besides the fact that `drat` appears to not be correlated in this model, we also observe a weak coefficient between `mpg` and `hp`, namely, $-0.032230$.

So, what is going wrong with this model?

## Testing for Correlations

We should first test whether there are any correlations in our independent variables:

```{r}
ivars <- mtcars[, c('wt', 'hp', 'drat')]
ivars_cor <- cor(ivars) # This computes Spearman's correlation
print(ivars_cor)
```

We should also compute the $p$ values for each correlation:

```{r}
# install.packages('Hmisc')
library(Hmisc)
ivars_cor_p <- rcorr(as.matrix(ivars))
print(ivars_cor_p$P) # Get just the p-values
```

So, as we see here, all independent variables are somehow correlated with strong enough $p$ values,
which means that the multicollinearity assumption might not hold. In particular, `drat`
appears strongly correlated with `wt`, which might imply that we should exclude one of the two variables. Also, there is a 
notable correlation between `hp` and `wt`, which also explains why we see such a small 
coefficient for `hp` in the above model.

We can also visualise the above using a correlogram:

```{r}
# install.packages('corrplot')
library(corrplot)
corrplot(ivars_cor, method = 'circle')
```

## Computing a New Model

In theory, larger values for `drat` should result to higher fuel consumption, i.e., lower `mpg`.
Inversely, smaller values for `drat` should result to higher `mpg`. However, in our previous
model the case was inverted since the regression coefficient was `1.615049` which is positive, 
that is, `drat` is found to positively affect `mpg`. One way to verify this is to also 
plot a correlogram including `mpg`, so:

```{r}
corrplot(cor(mtcars[, c('mpg', 'wt', 'hp', 'drat')]), method = 'circle')
```
We are now going to create a compound index taking into account `drat` and `hp` together by multiplying those, i.e.:

```{r}
cor_mlm <- lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp + drat + hp * drat, data = mtcars)
summary(cor_mlm)
```

Above we added an interaction term, as we say, where we add, alongside `drat` and `hp`, also `hp*drat`, 
i.e., their product. This is typically done in cases where we are interested into 
quantifying any interaction between two or more of our independent variables. However,
we should do so carefully, because adding such terms typically lowers the significance 
of other variables' coefficients, as we saw above. If that happens, this means that doing
so actually introduced more multicollinearity, i.e., made our model worse. So, this interaction,
should, in principle, be ignored.

Maybe, a different approach, might be to just drop `drat`, to begin with, and see with what sort of model we end up with:

```{r}
no_drat_mlm <- lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(no_drat_mlm)
```

Comparing this model with our first one, we see virtually no change, besides stronger $p$ 
values, which means that, in general, we should drop `drat` from our analysis.

Now, besides $p$ values and $R^2$, we should also look at Normal Q-Q plots and the 
rest of the useful plots we saw last time:

```{r}
plot(no_drat_mlm)
```

Starting with residuals vs fitted, we see a pretty much good picture, where residuals are 
nicely distributed. Also, the Q-Q plot seems to verify the normal residual distribution
assumption. Also, we see that the scale-location plot is quite good, looking like
randomly scattered points. The only plot that is a bit less good than the simple model
we crafted last time is the residuals vs leverage plot, where we see that some observations
have more leverage compared to our previous model and, also, residuals are a bit negatively 
distributed for lower values of leverage.

## Trying A Different Approach

Another approach to handle correlations between variables is to create a new variable based 
on highly correlated ones and create a simpler model. In our case, out of `wt`, `hp` and `drat`, 
we saw that `drat` is maybe irrelevant to `mpg` on the presence of the others, so we dropped it.
Also, we saw that `wt` and `hp` are quite positively correlated, so, we might create a 
new index by using both `wt` and `hp` and then use that to create a simple regression model. One simple
approach is to center our values for `wt` and `hp` by subtracting their mean values and then add them, i.e.:

```{r}
mwt <- mean(mtcars$wt)
mhp <- mean(mtcars$hp)
wt_hp_index <- (mtcars$wt - mwt + mtcars$hp - mhp)/2
index_data <- data.frame(mtcars$mpg, wt_hp_index)
colnames(index_data) <- c('mpg', 'wt_hp_index')
wt_hp_mlm <- lm(mpg ~ wt_hp_index, data = index_data)
summary(wt_hp_mlm)
```

Here, we get a solid $p$ value, but our model explains much less of the variance.
To see that, we can also plot the corresponding scatterplot:

```{r}
plot(index_data$wt_hp_index, index_data$mpg)
abline(wt_hp_mlm, col = 'red')
```

```{r}
plot(wt_hp_mlm)
```

So, for this model, we see that all metrics discussed above are more or less worse off than in the first and third models. Evidently, we should keep either the simple `mpg ~ wt` model or the multilinear `mpg ~ wt + hp` models, which do explain a lot of variance with most metrics being quite good.

# Working with Real Data

Let us now briefly try to create some models on real data, in particular, the ESS-pol dataset
we had extracted last time.


```{r}
ess_pol <- read.csv('ess_pol.csv', header = TRUE, sep = ',')
head(ess_pol)
```

To begin with, we should clean all dummy values, i.e., 7777, 8888, 9999 and so on:


```{r}
# We essentially look through each row, compute the sum of those that contain 9999 and keep only those which
# sum up to 0, i.e., those that do not contain 9999
for (v in c(5555, 6666, 7777, 8888, 9999)) {
  ess_pol <- ess_pol[rowSums(ess_pol == v, na.rm = TRUE) == 0, ]
}
```

Next, we create a simple MLM:

```{r}
ess_lm <- lm(formula = ess_data.ppltrst ~ ess_data.nwspol + ess_data.netusoft + ess_data.netustm, data = ess_pol)
summary(ess_lm)
plot(ess_lm)
```
This is evidently a bad model, mostly because we have not taken into account country plus some further data 
cleaning is required. So, you can have fun yourselves if you want to!
